steps.body: Multiplying by 10, 100, or 1,000 does not need a new fact — it takes a fact you own and scales it. 3 × 4 = 12 gives 30 × 4 = 120.
steps.narration: Multiplying by 10, 100, or 1,000 does not need a new fact — it takes a fact you own and scales it. 3 × 4 = 12 gives 30 × 4 = 120.

widget.prompt: Build a rectangle whose area is 120 using a side of 30. What is the other side?
widget.successFeedback: 30 × 4 = 120 — the fact 3 × 4 = 12, scaled by the ten inside 30.
widget.lowFeedback: Smaller than 120 — the rectangle has not reached the full area yet.
widget.highFeedback: Larger than 120 — one side has overshot the factor pair the prompt names.
widget.factorFeedback: That area is right, but not from the sides asked for — this rectangle must measure 30 by 4.

predict.reveal: 30 is three TENS, so the product is the basic fact taken ten times over.

cml.actionGoal: Split a factor into places, build each piece, and reassemble the whole for g4m powers ten.
invariants: Splitting a factor never changes the product: every piece of the split multiplies the other factor, and the pieces add back to exactly the same total, which is what makes g4m powers ten decomposable at all.
misconceptions: Adding only some of the partial products, dropping or inventing a zero when factors carry tens, or letting a remainder reach or exceed the divisor.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: If one partial product were left out, exactly how much of the total would go missing?

commonErrors.feedback: That dropped a zero. Each factor's zeros survive into the product — count them all.
That is one zero too many; multiply the basic fact first, then attach only the zeros the factors carry.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Split a factor into its places, multiply each part, and add every piece back.

widget.prompt: Why does knowing 3 × 4 = 12 immediately give you 30 × 4 = 120?

options.label: Because the factor is built from tens, so the basic fact is scaled by 10.
options.feedback: Correct — 30 is 3 tens, so the whole product is the basic fact taken ten times over.

options.label: Because a zero is always added to any product.
options.feedback: Zeros are not decoration; they appear only when a factor actually carries tens.

options.label: Because multiplication and addition give the same answer here.
options.feedback: 3 + 4 is 7, nowhere near 12 — the operations are genuinely different.

options.label: Because 30 and 3 are the same number.
options.feedback: They differ by a factor of ten, and that factor is exactly what scales the product.
